chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: You probably know that you need light to see things.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: But what exactly is light?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: What are its features?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And what makes them have so many different colors?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And what really happens when light gets brighter?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: What's really going on over there?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And what about those ultraviolet and infrared radiation

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: we say, which we can't see with our own eyes?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Is that light too?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So many different questions.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Let's get to the bottom of all these.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Light can be described using a wave model.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: We've talked about this before.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: When you disturb water at a particular point,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: it makes those molecules vibrate,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: which in turn makes the molecules surrounding it vibrate

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and so on and so forth.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And that's how the disturbance propagates

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: outwards as a ripple.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And if you have a continuous disturbance,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: like you have water dripping from a tap, for example,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: then you have a continuous wave or a periodic wave.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And the same thing looking from the side

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: looks somewhat like this.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And we've talked about various features of waves,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: like the speed at which the wave travels,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: the number of waves passing through a point

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: is what we call the frequency.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And the distance between consecutive peaks

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: or consecutive valleys, crescent troughs,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: we call it the wavelength.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And the amplitude represents the maximum change

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: from the equilibrium position.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Now guess what?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Light can be modeled exactly like this,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: meaning it has a wavelength, it has frequency,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: it has amplitude, and it has a particular speed.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: But wait, here's a question.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: In water waves, it's the water particles

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: that are going up and down, that's vibrating,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: producing a wave, right?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So the water acts as a medium.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: If you consider sound waves, the air acts as the medium.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: What about light?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: What is oscillating up and down?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: What is acting like a medium over here?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Well, we do see light traveling through air

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and then it traveling through glass.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So is that the medium for light?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: No, because light can also travel in vacuum.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: For example, this is how we get light from different stars.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: There is vast vacuum in between.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: There is absolutely no medium over there.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So the big question is then what's vibrating

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: when it comes to light?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: What's going up and down?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: To answer that question,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: let's look at a FET simulation over here.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: I have a charge over here

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and it's producing an electric field.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: An electric field is the reason why

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: if you place another charge over here,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: it experiences a force.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Similarly, magnets interact with each other

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: using magnetic fields, okay?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Now, here's a question.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: What's going to happen if I were to wiggle this charge?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Well, let's see.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: I'm gonna wiggle it.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Ooh, do you notice ripples going out

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: just like the ripples in the pond?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: This ripple going out is the ripples of electric field

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and there will also be magnetic field generated,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: which is not shown over here.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: But this ripples in electric and magnetic field

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: is what we call electromagnetic wave.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: It's a wave because you can see

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: that the disturbance is getting propagated.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: But what's wiggling over here?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Of course, the charge is wiggling over here,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: but what's the medium?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: What's wiggling when it comes to the waves?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: It's not matter, it's the field.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: The charge wiggling makes the electric

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and magnetic fields wiggle and that, you know,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: vibrations, that disturbance gets propagated outwards

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: as an electromagnetic wave

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and that electromagnetic wave is light, okay?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And so just like any wave,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: look, it will have properties like the speed.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So you can see this particular speed

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: at which the wave is emanating outwards.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: In vacuum, the speed of an electromagnetic wave

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: happens to be 300,000 kilometers per second.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: It's very fast, fastest thing in the universe.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And it also has frequency.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So for example, you can see this is low frequency,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: less number of waves traveling per second.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And then we can have high frequency,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: more number of waves traveling per second

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: because I'm wiggling it with higher frequency.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And then just like before, it can have amplitude.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: You can see amplitude represents the maximum change

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: from the equilibrium position.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So it has some amplitude now

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and I'm gonna reduce the amplitude.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Ooh, smaller amplitude, smaller wiggles.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Larger amplitudes, larger wiggles.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Let's try to make even larger amplitudes.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Oh my God, big wiggles.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So this is how we can model light

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: as an electromagnetic wave.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So what's oscillating up and down in the wave

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: is the electric and magnetic fields.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So now let's try to answer our original questions.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: What decides the color of the light?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Well, turns out it's the frequency.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Again, going back to our FET simulation,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: if we turn on light with low frequency,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: it tends to look red to us.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Low frequency light looks red to us.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And I have a graph over here

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: which shows the oscillations of the electric field.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And the sound is gonna help us get a sense of the frequency.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So here are the low frequency sound now.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: All right, low frequency.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Now let's see what happens if I turn up the frequency.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Here it goes.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Can you hear that?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: High frequency, right?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: It's oscillating much faster, high frequency.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: These are actually electromagnetic waves, okay?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So electric and magnetic fields are oscillating over here,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: but high frequency tends to be bluish,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: lower frequency tends to be reddish,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and all the other colors will come in between.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So it's the frequency that decides the color of the light.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So again, what we register as red color light

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: is basically light of lower frequency.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And what we register as bluish color lights

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: are lights of higher frequency.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: That's what decides the color.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Okay, what about the brightness?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: What decides the brightness?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Well, let's see.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Again, let me turn on the sound.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: The brightness is decided by the amplitude.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Let me make the amplitude very tiny and see what happens.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Here it goes.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: It's not so bright anymore.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: It becomes very dim.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Look at it.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Low amplitude means low brightness.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: On the other hand, if I were to increase the amplitude,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: let me just make it very, very high amplitude.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: When the sound increases just to let us know

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: that the amplitude has increased, this is high amplitude.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: This is a brighter light.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So the brightness comes from the amplitude.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: This means when the light is turning brighter,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: you can imagine its amplitude of the light

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: is becoming bigger and bigger.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: That's amazing, isn't it?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: But here's something that's even more mind boggling.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So what we understand so far is that

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: if you consider high frequency light

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: or light that has lower wavelength, smaller wavelengths,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: it tends to be bluish.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And as the wavelength becomes larger,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: the frequency tends to become smaller

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and the light tends to become redder and redder.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: But guess what?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: The visible light that we see is a very tiny portion

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: of the entire electromagnetic spectrum.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: This visible light has a wavelength

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: that is roughly of the size of a bacteria

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and our eyes are sensitive to that.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: But you can have wavelengths much larger

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and much smaller than this.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: So let's explore them.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: What happens if the wavelength becomes even larger

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: or if the frequency becomes even smaller than red?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Well, when the wavelength reaches the size of,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: you know, the thickness of a human hair, for example,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: we call that the infrared.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Now, we can't see it with our own eyes,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: but guess what?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Our bodies tend to send out infrared radiation all the time.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And so there are devices that can detect

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: this infrared radiation and then convert that

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: into visible light so we can see it.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: We call them thermal cameras

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and it can be used for night vision.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Okay, what happens if the wavelength becomes even larger

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: or if the frequency becomes even smaller?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Well, when the wavelength reaches the size of, say,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: a baseball, we now call it microwaves

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and they have the ability to heat up water.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And that's why microwave ovens exist

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and that's how they can heat up food

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: because they heat up the water in your food.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Okay, but what if it goes even larger?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Well, now if the wavelength reaches the size of buildings,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: for example, we call them radio waves.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: They can be used for long distance communications.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Okay, let's go on the other end of the spectrum.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: What happens if the wavelength becomes even smaller

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: than that of the visible light,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: meaning even higher frequency?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Well, if the wavelength becomes small enough,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: as small as, say, the viruses, for example,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: we call them ultraviolet waves.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And again, this is invisible to us,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: but turns out certain bees can see these waves.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: The sun also produces a lot of UV rays

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and they can cause damage to our DNA

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and that's the reason why we use sunscreens.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Okay, but what if the wavelength becomes even smaller?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: When they reach the size of, for example, molecules,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: we call them X-rays.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: One of their cool properties is they can penetrate skin,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: but they get absorbed by your bones

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: and that's why they can be used to take images

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: of your bones.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Okay, what if we go even smaller?

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Well, when the wavelength reaches the size

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: of the atomic nucleus, we call them gamma radiations.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelengths

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: or the highest frequency in the entire electromagnetic

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: spectrum and they're produced in nuclear reactions

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: like radioactive decays, for example.

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: And so there you have it,

chunks.title: Lecture
chunks.text: the entire electromagnetic spectrum.

chunks.title: Lecture
